title: Nehemiah 12:27–43
context: For the dedication of the wall, the Levites and singers are gathered to Jerusalem, and the priests and Levites purify themselves, the people, the gates, and the wall. Nehemiah sets two great companies giving thanks on the wall, one led by Ezra and the other followed by Nehemiah, which meet at God’s house. They offer great sacrifices and rejoice, “for God had made them rejoice with great joy,” and the joy of Jerusalem is heard far away; both traditions read the dedication and its joy as shared ground.

verses.text: At the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem, they sought the Levites out of all their places, to bring them to Jerusalem to keep the dedication with gladness, both with giving thanks and with singing, with cymbals, stringed instruments, and with harps.
verses.arminianNotes:
“At the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem, they sought the Levites out of all their places, to bring them to Jerusalem to keep the dedication with gladness.” Arminian readers note that the dedication is marked by thanksgiving and song.

The wall had been finished in fifty-two days (6:15); the time of the dedication is not stated.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the completed work dedicated to God with gratitude.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: work finished by God’s help is offered back to him with joy.

verses.text: The sons of the singers gathered themselves together, both out of the plain around Jerusalem and from the villages of the Netophathites;
verses.arminianNotes:
“The sons of the singers gathered themselves together, both out of the plain around Jerusalem and from the villages of the Netophathites.” Arminian readers note that singers come from the surrounding area.

The celebration draws the wider community.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the community gathering for worship.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the singers leave their homes to serve in a shared act of praise.

verses.text: also from Beth Gilgal and out of the fields of Geba and Azmaveth, for the singers had built themselves villages around Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes:
Singers come “from Beth Gilgal and out of the fields of Geba and Azmaveth, for the singers had built themselves villages around Jerusalem.” Arminian readers note that the singers lived near enough to serve.

The exact locations of some of these places are uncertain.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see a community arranged around service in Jerusalem.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the singers’ homes and their work in worship are connected.

verses.text: The priests and the Levites purified themselves; and they purified the people, the gates, and the wall.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The priests and the Levites purified themselves; and they purified the people, the gates, and the wall.” Arminian readers note that those who lead begin with their own purification.

The whole city is consecrated.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see holiness required for drawing near to God.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the dedication is not only a civic celebration but an act of worship that requires preparation.

verses.text: Then I brought the princes of Judah up on the wall, and appointed two great companies who gave thanks and went in procession. One went on the right hand on the wall toward the dung gate;
verses.arminianNotes:
“Then I brought the princes of Judah up on the wall, and appointed two great companies who gave thanks and went in procession.” Arminian readers note Nehemiah’s first-person account resuming.

One company goes toward the dung gate (cf. 2:13; 3:13–14).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the wall itself becoming a place of thanksgiving.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the route of the procession is described, though its exact course is uncertain.

verses.text: and after them went Hoshaiah, with half of the princes of Judah,
verses.arminianNotes:
The procession continues, “and after them went Hoshaiah, with half of the princes of Judah.” Arminian readers note that the leaders of the people join the procession.

Civil leaders walk with the singers.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the community’s leaders taking part in worship.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the procession unites leaders and people in giving thanks.

verses.arminianNotes:
The first company includes “Azariah, Ezra, and Meshullam.” Arminian readers note that the names continue the list of those in the first company.

This Ezra may be a priest of the same name rather than the scribe of 12:36.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise note the possibility of more than one Ezra in the list.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the procession includes many named participants.

verses.arminianNotes:
“Judah, Benjamin, Shemaiah, Jeremiah.” Arminian readers note that these may be names of individuals rather than tribes.

The list continues the first company.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also see a list of participants in the procession.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the record honors each one by name.

verses.text: and some of the priests’ sons with trumpets: Zechariah the son of Jonathan, the son of Shemaiah, the son of Mattaniah, the son of Micaiah, the son of Zaccur, the son of Asaph;
verses.arminianNotes:
The procession includes “and some of the priests’ sons with trumpets: Zechariah the son of Jonathan,” a line that continues to “the son of Asaph.” Arminian readers note the long genealogy linking Zechariah to Asaph.

Trumpets were used in celebration (cf. Num 10:10).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see continuity in the line of temple musicians.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the family of Asaph continued to serve in praise.

verses.text: and his brothers, Shemaiah, Azarel, Milalai, Gilalai, Maai, Nethanel, Judah, and Hanani, with the musical instruments of David the man of God; and Ezra the scribe was before them.
verses.arminianNotes:
His brothers play “with the musical instruments of David the man of God; and Ezra the scribe was before them.” Arminian readers note that Ezra leads the first company.

The instruments connect the celebration with David’s ordering of worship.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the scribe of the law leading a procession of praise.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the word of God and the worship of God go together.

verses.text: By the spring gate, and straight before them, they went up by the stairs of David’s city, at the ascent of the wall, above David’s house, even to the water gate eastward.
verses.arminianNotes:
They go “by the stairs of David’s city, at the ascent of the wall, above David’s house, even to the water gate eastward.” Arminian readers note the route through the old city of David.

The water gate is where the law had been read (8:1).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the procession passing places tied to Israel’s past.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the exact route is uncertain, but the procession honors Jerusalem’s history.

verses.text: The other company of those who gave thanks went to meet them, and I after them, with the half of the people on the wall above the tower of the furnaces, even to the wide wall,
verses.arminianNotes:
“The other company of those who gave thanks went to meet them, and I after them, with the half of the people on the wall.” Arminian readers note that Nehemiah walks behind the second company.

The two companies move toward each other.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the governor following in humility behind the singers.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the procession expresses unity in giving thanks.

verses.text: and above the gate of Ephraim, and by the old gate, and by the fish gate, the tower of Hananel, and the tower of Hammeah, even to the sheep gate; and they stood still in the gate of the guard.
verses.arminianNotes:
The second company passes the gate of Ephraim, the old gate, the fish gate, the towers of Hananel and Hammeah, “even to the sheep gate.” Arminian readers note gates mentioned in the rebuilding (3:1–6).

The walls built with effort are now walked in praise.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the completed wall used for worship.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the places of labor become places of thanksgiving.

verses.text: So the two companies of those who gave thanks in God’s house stood, and I and the half of the rulers with me;
verses.arminianNotes:
“So the two companies of those who gave thanks in God’s house stood, and I and the half of the rulers with me.” Arminian readers note that the processions end at the temple.

Worship is the goal of the rebuilding.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the processions converging at God’s house.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the wall serves the worship of God, not the reverse.

verses.text: and the priests, Eliakim, Maaseiah, Miniamin, Micaiah, Elioenai, Zechariah, and Hananiah, with trumpets;
verses.arminianNotes:
The second company includes “the priests, Eliakim, Maaseiah, Miniamin, Micaiah, Elioenai, Zechariah, and Hananiah, with trumpets.” Arminian readers note the priests’ role in the celebration.

Each is named.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see priests leading in praise.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the trumpets mark the joy of the occasion.

verses.text: and Maaseiah, Shemaiah, Eleazar, Uzzi, Jehohanan, Malchijah, Elam, and Ezer. The singers sang loud, with Jezrahiah their overseer.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The singers sang loud, with Jezrahiah their overseer.” Arminian readers note the energy of the singing.

Organized praise is led by an overseer.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see wholehearted praise offered to God.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: loud and joyful singing expresses gratitude for God’s help.

verses.text: They offered great sacrifices that day, and rejoiced, for God had made them rejoice with great joy; and the women and the children also rejoiced, so that the joy of Jerusalem was heard even far away.
verses.arminianNotes:
“They offered great sacrifices that day, and rejoiced, for God had made them rejoice with great joy.” Arminian readers note that the people’s joy is described as God’s gift.

Women and children join in, and “the joy of Jerusalem was heard even far away” (cf. Ezra 3:13).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see joy given by God (cf. 8:10).

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the people rejoice, and God is the source of their joy, which reaches beyond the city.
